text: Sergeant Otho Hays is the bravest man in the company, and the strangest. He goes out among the lodges when he is off duty and comes back with smoked fish and a new word or two. There is a chief from the Calumet village, Nau-non-gee, whom he has helped more times than I can count, with a mended gun lock, a blanket in a hard winter, a kind word when nobody else had one.

The men tease him that he will marry into the tribe. He only says that a man who lives among neighbours ought to know them. I think about that now, with the camps grown so large. Go and ask him what Nau-non-gee told him this summer. He will not answer me. Perhaps he will answer you.

tales.title: The run from Lee's farm
text: In April, John Kelso was out at Lee's farm on the South Branch, a free man then with his time served. Just before sunset a party of strangers who had come in friendly turned on the farm, and Liberty White and the Canadian Cardin were killed. Kelso and a boy ran. They ran the whole way down the river with the light going, and they came to the gate shouting.

That night every family in the settlement came into the fort. Four weeks later Kelso signed on again. He said he had done his running and now he would rather have a musket and a wall. He does not talk about it much. If you find him, do not ask him about the run. Ask him about the boy. He is proud of the boy.

tales.title: Wives in the barracks
text: Fielding Corbin did his five years, went out, and came back again, and this time he brought a wife. She is the steadiest person in the fort. She does the washing for half the company, she knows which of us drinks and which of us lies, and she has said to anyone who will listen that she will never be taken alive by anyone.

She is expecting a child. Corbin walks about like a man carrying a full bucket, careful of every step. He has asked to march beside her wagon tomorrow and the sergeant said yes before he had finished asking. If you want to see a soldier who is truly afraid, find Corbin. It is not for himself.

tales.title: Old Mott
text: The oldest man in the company is August Mortt, a German we call Old Mott. He has been a soldier since before some of our drummers were born. He fought somewhere in Europe, he says, though which war and on which side changes depending on the day.

What he will tell you, always the same, is that an army is safe while it stands still behind a wall and in danger the moment it walks out of one. He has said it every night this week. The young men tell him to hush. I do not. Old men who have lived through marches have earned the right to be gloomy. Go and find him if you want to hear about Europe. Bring tobacco.

tales.title: A father and son in one company
text: There are two John Smiths in this company, and they are father and son. The young one is a fifer. The old one is a private who pretends he does not watch the boy at drill, and who watches him at drill.

They enlisted three years apart, and they sleep in the same barracks room, and when the young one plays a sour note the old one coughs. That is the whole of their arguing. I asked the father once why he brought his son to the end of the earth. He said he did not bring him, the boy followed. Find the young Smith and ask him. He will roll his eyes and say his father followed him.

tales.title: The wagon detail
text: Elias Mills and William Moffett have the fort's wagon, and between the two of them they have the patience of a whole church. The oxen here are as stubborn as the officers, and the sand along the lake shore takes a wheel up to the hub.

Tomorrow the wagons will carry the children and the sick. Mills has been greasing axles since noon and checking every pin twice. He says a wagon that breaks on a march is a coffin with wheels. He means it as a joke, but nobody laughs. Find him at the wagon, if you like. He will show you how to hitch an ox, and he will not let you leave until you have done it properly.

tales.title: Captain Wells and his face
text: Yesterday Captain William Wells rode in from Fort Wayne with Miami men behind him. Wells was taken by the Miami as a boy and grew up among them, and married a daughter of Little Turtle himself. He has fought on both sides of every war in this country, and both sides say he is the best scout alive.

He is Mrs. Heald's uncle. He came to bring us home safe. I watched him talk to the captain in the yard, and I watched his face, which is a hard face to read. When he turned away from the captain he looked at the prairie for a long time. Find him if you can. Ask him what he thinks of tomorrow. I did not have the courage.

tales.title: The council and the cannon
text: Two days ago the captain went out to hold a council with the chiefs on the esplanade. The other officers would not go. They stayed in the blockhouse, and I heard one of them say the guns were trained on the council the whole time, in case of trouble.

I do not know if that is true. I know the chiefs could see the ports of the blockhouse, and a man can tell when he is being watched over a barrel. The captain promised them the goods of the factory, the guns and powder and the liquor, and they agreed to let us pass. Now the powder is in the well and the liquor is in the river. I keep thinking about how that council looked from the other side.

tales.title: A letter I cannot send
text: I wrote to my mother in May. It went east with the express rider, if he ever got there. I wrote to her again in July, but by then the war had come and nobody would carry it. I have it here inside my coat.

I told her about the lake, which is so big you would swear it was the sea, except that you can drink it. I told her about the cranes on the marsh, taller than a boy, that dance in the spring. I did not tell her that the post is surrounded or that the British took Mackinac in July without a shot. A letter is for the things you want your mother to keep. The rest you keep yourself.

tales.title: The fall of Mackinac
text: The worst news this summer did not come with an arrow. It came in a sentence. The British took Fort Mackinac on the seventeenth of July, and the American garrison there gave up without firing a shot because they did not even know there was a war.

Think on that. A fort on an island, in the middle of the straits, and it fell in a morning. If Mackinac can fall, so can Detroit, and if Detroit falls there is nothing between us and the whole British army but trees. The men from the camps heard the news before we did. That is how you know who your neighbours have been talking to.

tales.title: The red belt
text: This morning a runner came in to the camps carrying a big red belt. The interpreters went pale. A red belt is a call to war, and they say he came from Main Poc, the war leader who has gone over to the British and hates every American he has ever met.

The runner's name is Fox Running. He brought news of British victories in the north, and the young men gathered round him like flies on honey. I watched from the bastion. He did not look at the fort once, the whole time he was talking. That is how I knew he was talking about us. Find him if you dare. He will not lie to you about what he carries.

tales.title: The sick list
text: Every soldier here has had the ague. You shake until your teeth knock, then you burn, then you shake again. Doctor Van Voorhis doses us with bark and calomel and tells us it is the marsh air. He is a young man from Fishkill on the Hudson, and he writes long letters home about how this country will be rich one day.

He is right, I think. But he will not be here to see it, and neither will I. The sick are to ride in the wagons tomorrow. The doctor has been up two nights counting blankets and bandages. If you find him, tell him to sleep. He listens to no one, but he might listen to a stranger.

tales.title: An old friend from the north
text: Sergeant Crozier has been here since 1808, and in that time he has made friends you would not expect. There is a Chippewa man from up the lake who comes to see him every summer, and the two of them sit by the river and smoke and say almost nothing for an afternoon.

I asked him once what they talk about. He said they talk about fish, and weather, and how foolish young men are, which is the same talk old soldiers have everywhere. I believe a friend like that is worth more than a cannon in a bad week. Find the sergeant and ask him if his friend has come this year. Watch his face when he answers.

tales.title: The linden birds
text: William Griffith was a settler until April. After the killings at Lee's farm he joined the army right here at Chicago and he is a sergeant already, because he can read and write and does not panic.

He told me something I cannot get out of my head. One of the chiefs, a friend to the fort, told him that the linden birds had been singing in his ears. Griffith did not understand it at first. Then the interpreter explained. It means the chief has heard things he cannot say out loud, warnings carried on the wind. Griffith asked him what the birds said. The chief only looked at him. Find Griffith and ask him who the chief was.

tales.title: On the night watch
text: I had the watch on the north-west blockhouse two nights ago. You can see the river from there and the Kinzie house beyond it, with its poplars, and past that the dark of the prairie. That night the prairie was not dark. There were fires out there, more than I could count, all the way to the trees.

You hear things on a night watch. A dog. A drum, far off. Singing, sometimes, that rises and falls and stops all at once. I am not a superstitious man, but I said a prayer up there that I have not said since I was a boy. When the relief came up the ladder I nearly shot him.

tales.title: The man who will not go
text: Antoine Ouilmette was here before the fort was built, or so he says, and his wife is Potawatomi. He works the portage for Mr. Kinzie, carrying packs across the mud to the Des Plaines. He never joined the militia and he is not marching tomorrow.

He told me he is going to stay home. Just that. Stay home and mind his garden. The officers think he is a fool or a traitor. I think he is the one man in Chicago who knows exactly where he belongs. If you want to know how a man can be at home in a place like this, ask him. He will offer you a pipe and talk about the portage until you fall asleep.

tales.title: Cleaning a musket
text: Watch a soldier clean his musket on a day like this and you will learn everything you need to know about him. One man scours the barrel until it shines like a spoon. One man does it in three strokes and goes to find his dinner. One man takes the lock apart and puts it back together four times, because his hands need something to do.

I am the third kind today. Tomorrow we carry twenty-five rounds each. The rest of the powder went into the well. The captain says we must not leave anything for our enemies. The men from the camps say the captain promised it to them. Both of them are right, and that is the trouble.

tales.title: The fort garden
text: We planted the garden in May, when we were all living inside the walls after the killings in April. Beans, cabbages, turnips, a row of potatoes, and corn the way the Potawatomi women showed us, in hills. The women across the river laughed at our hills. They said we planted like men who had never been hungry.

The corn is coming in now. Fine ears, tall as a man. And we are leaving it. Some fellow from the camps will eat my turnips this winter, and I hope they choke him, and I hope they feed his children. Both at once. That is how a man feels when he leaves his garden.

tales.title: Why I enlisted
text: I enlisted at seventeen because a recruiting sergeant in Pennsylvania bought me supper and told me about the West. He did not mention the mosquitoes. He did not mention the fevers, or the winters, or the way the wind comes off the lake in January and goes straight through a wool coat as if it were paper.

But he did not lie about the West. I have seen buffalo on the far prairie, a dark smudge moving like a cloud shadow. I have seen the lake turn green and gold and grey in a single afternoon. If I get home I will tell my brothers about it, and they will not believe a word.

tales.title: The order of march
text: The order of march came down this afternoon. Captain Wells and some of his Miami in front. Then the regulars. Then the wagons with the women and children and the sick, and the militia with them. Then the rest of the Miami at the back. We go down the beach, along the lake, toward Fort Wayne, a hundred and fifty miles.

Somebody asked the sergeant what music we would march out to. He said the band will play what the captain orders. Somebody else said they had heard it would be the Dead March. The sergeant told him to hold his tongue. Nobody spoke for a long time after that.

tales.title: Bread for the road
text: The bakers have been at the oven since before dawn, making hard bread for the march. Fifty-odd soldiers, a dozen militia, the women and the children, all to be fed for a hundred and fifty miles, and the factory's flour is mostly gone to the camps.

I carried sacks for them this morning. The baker is a sour man who has never said a kind word to me, but he slipped me a soft roll still hot from the oven and told me to eat it quick before the captain saw. I did. It was the best thing I have eaten at this post. Funny, what you remember.

tales.title: The women will ride
text: Sergeant Holt has given his wife his own horse for the march, and he has been teaching her to ride it astride, like a man, so she can stay on in the sand. She is not a natural horsewoman. Twice today I saw her slide off and twice she got back on, red in the face, and told him to stop laughing.
He was not laughing. He was standing with his hand on the bridle, very still. Find Sergeant Holt if you like. He will tell you she rides better than he does. That is a lie, but it is a good one.

tales.title: The twelve of the militia
text: After the killings in April, the captain made soldiers of every grown man in the settlement who was not already one. Twelve of us. Thomas Burns is our sergeant, an old soldier himself who stayed on here when his time was up and married a widow with a houseful of children.

We drill on the parade with the regulars, and they laugh at us, because we march like farmers going to market, which is what we are. But every one of us has a family inside these walls. A man fights differently when the wagon behind him holds his own children. Find Burns. He will tell you we are getting better. That is very nearly true.

tales.title: Carried on her bed
text: The night we all came into the fort in April, Mrs. Burns had given birth only the day before. She could not walk. So Mr. Kinzie and his men carried her down to the boat on her bed, mattress and blankets and baby and all, and rowed her across the river with the newborn in her arms.

I helped hold the lantern. She did not make a sound the whole way except to tell the boatmen to mind the baby's head. The baby is fat now and has a voice like a bugle. If you see Mrs. Burns, tell her I said the baby takes after her. She will know who it was.

tales.title: Lee's boy
text: Charles Lee feeds the fort. His farm out on the South Branch grows the wheat and the beef, or it did until April, when the farm was attacked and his men killed. His boy got away that day, running down the river to the fort with the alarm.

Lee has not been back to the farm since. He drills with the militia and he looks at the South Branch every evening from the walls. His boy marches beside him. They are very alike, both quiet, both stubborn. Ask Lee about the farm and he will tell you about next year's wheat as if there will be a next year. I hope he is right.

black_jim.title: The Kinzie boat
text: They call me Black Jim. I work for Mr. Kinzie, and whether the law calls me free or something else is a thing I keep to myself. I do the heavy work: wood, water, the boats. Tomorrow I will be in the bow of the family boat.

I have checked every plank. I have put an axe under the seat where my hand can find it. The children will be behind me, and Mrs. Kinzie, and the nurse. If anybody comes at that boat, he will have to come past me first. Go and tell young Johnny that Jim is ready. He will feel better. So will I.

black_partridge.title: The medal
text: Seventeen years ago at Greenville, General Wayne hung this medal on my chest, and I promised peace with the Americans. I have kept that promise every day since. I have held back my young men. I have fed the soldiers when they were hungry.

Tonight I am going to the captain's house with the interpreter, and I will give him back his medal. I will tell him the truth: the linden birds have been singing in my ears. The young men will not be held, and I will not wear the sign of a friendship I cannot keep. It is the hardest thing I have ever done. But a man who wears a lie on his chest is worse than an enemy. Go to the captain's quarters tonight. You will see me there.

blackbird.title: The war leader
text: The French call me Letourneau. My people call me Black Bird. In the spring I was with Pepper's band on the Au Sable, and last year I sat in council with the Americans at Peoria, and I listened to their promises, and I watched them take the Wabash.

The young men look to me now. That is a heavy thing. A war leader does not choose the war. The war chooses him, and then he must decide how it will be fought, and how it will end. Whatever happens tomorrow, I have told the young men this: when it is done, it is done. A man who has given up is not to be harmed. Remember I said it. Tell the captain, if you see him.

burns_mrs.title: Carried in my bed
text: I had my baby the night before the alarm in April. The next evening the Kinzie men came running and said the farm had been attacked and everyone must go into the fort. I could not stand. So they picked up my bed, with me in it and the baby in my arms, and carried it down to the boat and across the river and in through the gate.

I have been in the fort ever since, with all my children, and the youngest of them was a day old when we came. Tomorrow we go in the wagon. My husband marches beside it. Find him. Tell him the baby has stopped crying. It has not. Tell him anyway.

burns_thomas.title: Sergeant of the militia
text: I served my time in this fort and then I stayed, because I liked the country and I liked a widow named Mrs. Cooper, and she liked me well enough. Now I have a house on the north bank with a cow in it, and a wife, and a houseful of her children who are mine now, and a new baby of our own born the night before we all ran into the fort.

The captain made me sergeant of the twelve. We are farmers with muskets. Tomorrow I will march with them beside the wagons that carry my family. Go and see my wife. Tell her I will be close by. Tell her the cow will be fine.

chandonnai_jean_baptiste.title: Between the lodges and the books
text: I am Mr. Kinzie's clerk. I keep his books, I count his furs, and I carry his words to the camps and their words back to him. My mother's people are Potawatomi and my father's people are French, and so I am welcome everywhere, and trusted nowhere entirely.

Tomorrow Mr. Kinzie has asked me to take care of his family in the boat. I have told him I will. I have also told my cousins in the camps that this family is under my protection. Some of them listened. Whatever happens tomorrow, I will spend the day walking between the two sides with my hands open. It is the only thing I know how to do.

cicely.title: My son
text: My name is Cicely. That is the only name anyone has ever written for me. I came here with the captain and his wife from Louisville, on horseback, with my baby in my arms. I keep the captain's house. I cook and wash and sew and keep my mouth shut, which is what is wanted of me.

But I will tell you about my son, because you asked. He is just beginning to talk. He says no to everything and laughs when he says it. He holds onto my finger so tight in the night that I wake with it numb. Tomorrow I will carry him. Whatever else the world has decided I am, I am his mother. Nobody can write that away.

corbin_fielding.title: I came back for her
text: I did my five years and went out, and then I came back and signed on again, because my wife would not live anywhere but here, and a soldier's pay is better than none. She does the washing for the company. She is expecting our child.

She has told everyone that she will never be taken. I believe her. I asked the sergeant to let me march beside the wagon tomorrow, and he said yes before I finished. Go and see her. Tell her I have the blankets packed, and her good shawl. She will say I packed them wrong. She will be right.

griffith_william.title: A settler turned sergeant
text: I was a settler here until April. When the killings came at Lee's farm, I walked into the fort and put my name down. By June I had stripes. That tells you how many men here can read.

A chief came to me this summer, a friend to the fort, and said the linden birds had been singing in his ears. I did not understand until the interpreter explained it: he had heard warnings he could not say aloud. I think it was Black Partridge, though he did not say so. If you find him, tell him Griffith understood.

hays_otho.title: A friend in the camps
text: I signed on in April of last year and I am a sergeant now. I am not a clever man, but I have always believed that if you live beside people you ought to be decent to them. So I have been decent to Nau-non-gee of the Calumet village. I mended his gun. I gave him a blanket in the cold.

This summer he does not meet my eye. Somebody told me what he said about the officers' wives and his cornfield. I do not believe he meant it. I believe he is a man caught in a hard year, like me. Go and find him if you can. Tell him Sergeant Hays has not forgotten him either.

heald_nathan.title: My orders
text: I am a soldier, and a soldier obeys. General Hull wrote that I am to evacuate the post if it is practicable, and give the factory's goods to the Indians, and march for Fort Wayne. I have read the letter twenty times. If practicable. Two words, and my whole command hangs on them.

Mr. Kinzie thinks I should stay. Some of my officers think so too, and say it to my back. But I have five days of argument behind me, and four hundred warriors outside, and orders in my pocket. I have chosen to march. I will not make a speech about it. Tomorrow, at nine o'clock, the gate opens. I pray I am right.

heald_nathan.title: Rebekah
text: I married Rebekah Wells in Kentucky last May, and we rode here together on horseback with her servant and the servant's child, through a month of forest. I had told her it was a hard post. She said she was a Wells, and the Wells family did not choose easy places.

This spring we lost our son. There was no one here who knew what to do. She has not complained once, not of the baby, not of the fort, not of me. Tomorrow she will ride beside the column with her uncle in front. If you meet her, you will understand why I am more afraid for her than for any man in the company.

heald_rebekah.title: I will ride
text: My uncle William came yesterday from Fort Wayne with his Miami to take us home. I have not seen him since I was a girl. He looks older and harder, and he hugged me in front of the whole garrison as if I were still twelve.

Nathan wanted me to go in the Kinzies' boat. I said no. I came here on a horse and I will leave on one. My uncle smiled at that, the first smile I have seen on him. He told me to keep my horse close to his. I will. If you find him, tell him I am ready. He worries, though he would rather die than say it.

helm_linai.title: The second lieutenant
text: I came here from Detroit as second in command and married the trader's stepdaughter, and some of the officers have not forgiven me for being happy. Margaret is the bravest girl in the Northwest. She has told me she will ride beside the column tomorrow, and I have stopped arguing.

I disagreed with the captain about the march. I said so once, properly, and then I held my tongue, because that is what an officer does. Tomorrow I will march where I am ordered and fight if I must. If you see Margaret, do not tell her I am afraid. Tell her I said she rides better than I do. It is true.

helm_margaret.title: I will not leave him
text: My mother wants me in the boat with her and the little ones. I told her no. I married Linai Helm last year, and I am going where he is going. I am seventeen and I can ride as well as any soldier in this fort, and I can shoot.

My mother looked at me for a long time and then she kissed me and said, then ride well. That is all. She knows the camps better than anyone and she did not tell me I was safe. Go and find my husband. He will pretend to be cross with me for not going in the boat. He is not. He is proud. So am I.

keepotah.title: The boat at the river mouth
text: I am Kee-po-tah. I have visited the Kinzies many times. I was at their house when the American general Harrison came through and we met, years ago. I like Mrs. Kinzie. She speaks to me as an equal, and she was a captive herself once, raised among the Senecas, so she understands more than the others.

Tomorrow, when the soldiers march, I will be at the mouth of the river with another man, standing beside their boat. Nobody will touch it while I am there. Go and tell Mrs. Kinzie not to be afraid. She will pretend she was not. But she will hear it.

kelso_john.title: The run
text: I was done with the army in December of 1810. A free man, working where I pleased. In April I was at Lee's farm when the strangers came. Before sunset they turned on the farm. I took Lee's boy by the arm and we ran.

We ran down the river bank with the light going, through the brush, through the water when we had to. We did not look back. At the gate I could not speak, so the boy spoke for both of us. A month later I put my name on the army's paper again. A man who has run once does not want to run again. Find Lee and tell him his boy was braver than I was.

kinzie_eleanor.title: I was a captive once
text: When I was a little girl in Pennsylvania, the Senecas came to our farm and carried me away. I lived among them for years. The old chief adopted me as his own daughter and I loved him, and when my family finally found me and took me home, I cried for him.

So I do not look at the camps the way the officers do. I know there are kind people out there, and grieving people, and angry people, the same as in any town. Tomorrow I take my little ones in the boat. My Margaret will ride with her husband. I have told her all I can. Go and find her. Tell her that her mother is watching from the water.

kinzie_john_elder.title: I told the captain not to go
text: When General Hull's letter came, I told Captain Heald what I thought. Stay inside the walls, I said. You have provisions for six months and powder enough. Or go at once, tonight, before the camps fill. But do not wait, and do not promise the chiefs what you will not give.

He waited. He promised. And then, on my own advice, he poured away the liquor and the powder he had promised, because I would not have the young men armed and drunk at our backs. So I have helped to make the anger I warned him against. That is the trouble with good advice given halfway. Tomorrow I will walk with the soldiers, and my wife and children will go in the boat. Ask the captain what he makes of me now.

kinzie_john_elder.title: Lalime
text: You will have heard about Lalime. Everyone has. On the seventeenth of June, at sunset, outside the gate. I will not tell you what words passed between us. That is between me and him and God. I will tell you that I came away with a wound in my neck and he did not come away at all.

A friend took me up the shore to Milwaukee that night, and I waited there until word came that the officers thought it was a fair fight and I could come home. He is buried in front of my own house, inside a fence. I look at it every morning. A man ought to look at what he has done.

kinzie_john_h_1812.title: I am nine
text: I am nine and I am the eldest, so I have to help Mama with the little ones in the boat tomorrow. Ellen is six and Maria is four and Robert is only two, and he screams if you take his spoon away.

Papa says I must be the man of the boat until he comes back, because he is going to walk with the soldiers. I said I would. I have my knife and a piece of maple sugar in my pocket. Josette sewed pockets into all our clothes with corn and sugar inside, in case we get hungry. Mama does not know. Do not tell her.

laframboise_josette_1812.title: The children's nurse
text: I am Josette. My mother's people are Ottawa, from up the lake, and my father was a French trader, so I speak to the Kinzie children in three languages and they answer me in a fourth that is all their own.

Tomorrow I will sit in the boat with Mrs. Kinzie and the little ones while the soldiers march. I am frightened, but children can smell fear, so I am not allowed to be. I have sewn food into their clothes and taught Johnny a word to say if a stranger comes near the boat. Go and ask him to say it for you. He is very proud of it.

lee_charles.title: My farm on the South Branch
text: I came here about seven years ago and took up land on the South Branch, and I made the first real farm in this country. Wheat, cattle, hogs. I fed this fort. My family lived down by the river mouth and my men worked the farm.

In April a party of strangers came to the farm friendly and then turned on my men. Liberty White and the Canadian Cardin were killed. My boy got away, running all the way down the river to the fort with John Kelso. I have not been back. Go and find Kelso. Thank him for me. I have tried, and the words do not come out right.

main_poc_runner.title: The red belt
text: I am a runner. I have come a long way from Main Poc with this belt and with news. Mackinac belongs to the British. The Americans' general Hull has crossed into Canada and run back again like a frightened deer. Detroit will fall. The British father has said to all his children: now is the time.

I have told this at every fire tonight. The old men look at the belt and say nothing. The young men touch it. A belt does not make a war. It only says, the war is here, will you come? Every man must answer for himself. Most of them already have.

naunongee.title: The officers' wives at play
text: In the spring I watched the officers' wives playing games on the parade, running and laughing like girls. I said to the interpreter: they are amusing themselves very much now. It will not be long before they are hoeing in my cornfield. He went white and told everyone.

I meant it, and I did not mean it. That is what men say in a hard year. And yet there is a sergeant in that fort, Hays, who has been kinder to me than my own cousins. He mended my gun. He gave me a blanket. I do not know what tomorrow will make of the two of us. Go and find him. Tell him Nau-non-gee remembers the blanket.

nuscotnemeg.title: The Mad Sturgeon
text: They call me the Mad Sturgeon. The Americans in the Illinois settlements blame me for killings two summers ago, and they have asked the chiefs to give me up. The chiefs have not. My daughter is married to Billy Caldwell, who is half Irish and rides with Tecumseh now. So you see, everybody in this country is related to everybody else.

I do not pretend to be a peaceful man. I have seen too much of what peace with the Americans brings: a medal, a treaty, and the land gone. Tomorrow I will be on the beach. Do not look for me afterwards. If I live, I will be somewhere on the Des Plaines, and you will not find me unless I want you to.

ouilmette_antoine.title: I am staying home
text: I came here in 1790, before the fort, before the Americans, when this was a river and a few houses and the lake. I have carried goods over the portage for Mr. Kinzie for years. My wife Archange is Potawatomi, and her people are my people.

Everybody is leaving tomorrow. The captain asked me to join the militia, and I said no, I am not a soldier. Tomorrow when they march I am going to stay home and mind my garden. When it is over, whatever it is, I will still be here. Go and meet my wife. She will feed you. She feeds everybody.

ronan_george.title: Straight from West Point
text: I came here from West Point in March of last year, the youngest officer at the post. I have read every manual on infantry tactics ever printed, and I have learned that none of them were written for a fort on a sandbar with four hundred warriors outside.

The older officers think I am green. They are right. But I have said what I think of the march, out loud, in front of the captain, and he did not like it. I may have been rude. If I was, I am not sorry. Tomorrow I will march where I am told and I will not run. Tell the captain I said so.

topenebe.title: My old friend's family
text: I am Topenebe, chief of the St. Joseph people. I have known John Kinzie since before this fort was built. My sister married the trader Burnett. Our families have eaten from the same kettle for twenty years.

I cannot stop the young men. No one can now. But I can tell my friend what I hear, and I can stand near his boat when the time comes. Keep your family on the water, I told him. Do not let them go with the soldiers along the shore. He listened. He is a stubborn man, but he is not a fool. Go and ask him if I am right. He will not say. But he will put his family in the boat.

van_voorhis_isaac.title: A young doctor's prospects
text: I came here from Fishkill on the Hudson, a young doctor, and last year I wrote home that this country would one day be the garden of the world. I still believe it. The soil is so black and so deep that you could plant a walking stick and get a tree.

Since Mr. Irwin left I have kept the keys of the factory, and this week I have given away every bolt and kettle in it, on the captain's order. I told the captain what I thought of the march. He listened politely, which is how captains listen to young doctors. Tomorrow I will ride with the wagons and the sick. If you see the captain, tell him the medicine chest is packed.

waubansee.title: A small band on the Fox River
text: I lead a small band on the Fox River, thirty men in the spring, fewer now that some have gone south to the British. We are not a great people. We hunt and plant and trade with Kinzie, who has always been fair with us.

My young men want to be part of what is coming. I understand them. When the whole world is moving, a young man cannot stand still. But I have told them: Kinzie and his family are not to be touched. Whatever happens on the beach, the trader's house is ours to guard. Some of them laughed. I did not laugh. They will see.

wells_william.title: Why I came
text: I came because my niece is here. That is the whole of it. When I heard Hull had ordered the post abandoned, I knew what the road along the lake would look like with four hundred young men watching it. I got thirty Miami who would come and I rode.

I was a Miami before I was anything else, and I know what they are saying in the camps tonight, because I have said it myself, long ago, about other forts. I would have stayed behind the walls. The captain has made his decision. So I will lead the column out, in front. Tomorrow I am going to paint my face. You will know what that means, if you know the old ways. If you do not, it is better that you do not ask.

winnemeg.title: The letter I carried
text: I am Winnemeg, the Catfish, of the St. Joseph River. Two years ago I kept my people out of Tecumseh's confederacy, because I believed peace was the stronger road. So when General Hull wanted a messenger to Chicago, he chose me. I walked here with his letter, and I gave it to the captain, and I told Kinzie what I thought.

Go now, I said, at once, tonight, before the others come. Leave everything. Or stay behind your walls and do not come out. Do not wait. Do not give away the guns. Do not promise. The captain did all of those things. I have done what a friend can do. Ask Kinzie. He heard every word.

asks.q: What is this river called in your language?
a: Shikaakwa, near enough, for the wild leek that grows thick along its banks in spring. The smell of it hangs over the marsh in April. The French wrote it down as Chicagou and the Americans dropped the end. Chandonnai, the trader's clerk, can say it the old way and the French way and the American way. Ask him to say all three.

For a village, no: too wet, too many mosquitoes, the ground floods every spring. For a crossing, the best on the lakes. Every canoe from the north going down to the Illinois comes through here and over the portage. Whoever sits at this river mouth hears everything first.

more.q: Is that why the Americans built here?
a: Yes. They did not build here for the leeks.

asks.q: That is a fine horse. Where did it come from?
a: Traded from the Sauk, who had it from somebody on the Missouri, who had it from somebody further west. A horse walks a long way before it reaches you. I gave four good beaver packs and a gun for him, and I have never regretted it.

He has a name I will not tell a stranger, and a name I call him when he will not cross water, which I will not tell you either. He is fast on the prairie and stupid in the woods. Like some men I know.
Everyone who has a horse will be on it tomorrow, one way or another. The soldiers are walking. Think about that.

asks.q: Is everyone in the camps Potawatomi?
a: Most, but not all. There are Ottawa from the north, and Ojibwe, and a few Winnebago and Kickapoo who came to see what would happen. We three, Potawatomi, Ottawa and Ojibwe, call ourselves brothers: the three fires. We came down the lakes together long ago, and we still speak nearly the same language.

more.q: Do the brothers agree about the Americans?
a: Brothers never agree. The Ojibwe in the far north barely see an American from one year to the next. The Ottawa trade with the British at Mackinac. We Potawatomi live next to the Americans. We have the most to gain and the most to lose.
They are angry and they are not our relatives, and when something bad happens, people say: the Winnebago did it. Sometimes it is true. It is very convenient for everybody else when it is.

asks.q: Where do your people get guns?
a: From the traders, mostly the British ones at Mackinac and Malden, and from the Americans here when they were selling. Every autumn a man needs powder, lead, flints and a gun that works. Without them his family does not eat in winter. A gun is a hoe for meat.

more.q: Do the British give them free?
a: The British give presents every year: guns, blankets, kettles, silver, tobacco. They call it keeping the friendship bright. The Americans give presents too, but fewer, and they want land at the end of it. A man notices which friend asks for nothing back.
I can change a flint and clean the pan. For anything more there is a smith at the fort who mends guns for the villages. Mended them, I should say. He will not mend any more of them, now.

asks.q: Where is your village?
a: On the Kankakee, three days' walk south and east, where the river runs slow through the marsh and the wild rice grows. Forty lodges in summer. In winter we scatter to the hunting grounds and come back in spring to plant.

more.q: Is it near anyone I might meet?
a: Waubansee's people are on the Fox, west of us. He is here, by the river with his men. He is a war leader, but a careful one. He will tell you his own mind about tomorrow, and not anybody else's. Go and find him.

more.q: Will you go home after this?
a: After tomorrow, yes. Whatever happens tomorrow, my wife wants the corn in, and the corn does not care about the Americans.

asks.q: You speak French?
a: Enough to trade and enough to swear. My mother's sister married a Frenchman at St. Joseph, so I grew up with French cousins who ate their corn on a plate and crossed themselves before thunder. Half the people at this river have a French grandfather somewhere.

The French here have no country to take sides for. Their king is gone, their flag is gone, their priests are mostly gone. They have their families, which are half ours, and their trade, which is all of ours. They will stand with whoever lets them keep both.

more.q: Who is the most French person here?
a: Ouilmette, across the river, who says he will stay when the Americans go. He came here as a boatman more than twenty years ago and married into the Potawatomi and never left. He thinks nobody will hurt him. He may be right. We have known him a long time.

asks.q: What is that belt of beads?
a: Wampum. Small shell beads, white and purple, strung and woven into a belt. A belt carries words. When a message goes from one nation to another, the belt goes with it, so the people who receive it know the message is true and the sender means it.

I can tell you what some of the patterns mean: the white road is peace, the dark is grief or war. To know what a particular belt says, you have to ask the man who carried it and heard the words spoken over it. The beads hold the promise. The man holds the words.

more.q: Has a belt come this summer?
a: Many. From Tecumseh, from the British, from the villages on the Wabash. Some white, some dark. I will not tell you which ones my village accepted. You can guess.

asks.q: Did you make that canoe?
a: My uncle and I, two summers ago. Birch bark from the north, sewn with spruce root, sealed with pitch, over cedar ribs. A bark canoe weighs no more than a man can carry on his shoulders, which is why we can cross the portage with it and the French can, and the Americans with their heavy boats cannot.

Dugouts are for slow water: a whole tree trunk, burned and scraped out. Heavy, but they last, and you cannot tear them on a snag. Most of the canoes on this river are dugouts now. The good birch is far to the north.
Not tonight. Tonight nobody goes out on the river who does not have to. Ask me in a better summer.

asks.q: What do you think of the trader Kinzie?
a: Shawneeawkee, we call him, the silversmith, because he worked silver when he first came among us, and still makes brooches for our women. He has lived at this river longer than the fort. He knows every family and what every family owes him, to the muskrat.

He is the friend of every man who pays him. That is not an insult. That is what a trader is. But he also feeds people in bad winters and does not ask. Some of the chiefs have said quietly that his family must not be harmed tomorrow. Go and look at his house. You will see warriors sitting in front of it who are not there to attack it.

more.q: What about the man he killed?
a: Lalime, the interpreter, in June, by the fort. They had quarrelled for years. Some say Lalime drew first. The captain did nothing. Kinzie went away for a while and came back. Among my people, a death is answered by a gift to the family or by another death. The Americans seem to have no way at all.

asks.q: Is there a sacred place near here?
a: There are places along the lake and up the rivers where people go to be alone and hear what the spirits want of them. I will not tell you where. A sacred place told to a stranger is no longer a place, only a spot on the trader's map.

That the lake is alive and should be spoken to before you put a canoe on it. That a man leaves tobacco when he takes something from the land. That is all I will say, and it is more than most of my relatives would.

asks.q: Who is the man everyone stops talking around?
a: A runner of Main Poc's band, from the Kankakee, wearing the red belt. Main Poc is the war leader born with a hand that has no fingers, whose power is so strong even other war leaders are afraid of him. He has gone to the British at Malden. His runners carry his words to the camps here.

That the Americans are a sickness and the only cure is to drive them out of the whole country. That the Great Spirit gave the land to the nations and no paper can take it away. Many young men here have heard those words all summer.

more.q: Should I talk to the runner?
a: You can try. He will not hurt you here, in front of everyone. But he will look at you as if he is counting you. Go and see for yourself, and do not stay long.

asks.q: What is wild rice?
a: A grass that grows in shallow water, taller than a man, with grain at the top. In late summer we pole canoes into the rice beds and bend the stalks over and knock the grain into the bottom of the canoe with two sticks. It is the best food there is. The Ojibwe live on it.
Nearly. In a few weeks, the rice on the Kankakee will be ripe. My sisters are already there, waiting. I came here for the goods the captain promised. I wish I had stayed with my sisters.

Parch it in a kettle over the fire, then dance on it in a pit to loosen the husks, then winnow it in a birch basket on a windy day. Then boil it with maple sugar or with duck. If you ever eat it, you will not want bread again.

asks.q: Do Potawatomi women marry Frenchmen?
a: Many do. Archange, across the river, is married to the Frenchman Ouilmette, and her father was a Frenchman too, and her mother one of us. A trader with a Potawatomi wife has a hundred relatives in the camps who will trade with him and nobody else. That is good for him. A Potawatomi woman with a trader husband has kettles and cloth and a house with a floor. That is good for her.

Both, often. Archange and her husband have been together since before the fort was built and have a house full of children. Go and see her. She will laugh at your question and give you something to eat.

more.q: Will she go with the soldiers?
a: No. She will stay with her husband and her children, on her own river, with her own relatives all round her. Who would harm her? Half the young men in the camps call her aunt.

asks.q: What are you weaving?
a: A mat of cattail leaves, for the winter lodge. I cut the leaves in summer, dry them, and sew them together with a bone needle and basswood cord. Six of these will cover a lodge. Twenty mats a summer, every summer, since I was twelve.

Not hard. Long. You do it while you talk, while you watch the children, while the men argue. My grandmother said that a woman's hands remember what her head forgets. I do not need to look at the needle any more.
The trader's wife bought two for her floor. She said they were warmer than any rug from Detroit. She was right.

asks.q: Where is your family?
a: My husband is in the council tonight with the other men. My mother is in the lodge with my children. My brother is somewhere with the young men by the river, painting his face, and I have not been able to talk to him all day.

To remember who fed him last winter. The soldiers' wives gave us flour when the corn ran out in March. To remember the children in the fort are children. He knows all that. Whether he listens to it tomorrow, I cannot tell you.

asks.q: How far did you ride to get here?
a: From Fort Wayne, at the head of the Maumee, along the old trail by the St. Joseph River and round the bottom of the lake. Something like a hundred and fifty miles. We did it in less than a week, pushing hard. Apekonit said every day counted.

Hot. Flies. Rivers to swim the horses across. And the people in the villages along the way watching us and saying nothing. We knew what they were thinking: those are the Miami who ride with the Americans. Not all of my relatives approve.
Going back we will be walking at the pace of oxen and wagons and children. It will take two weeks. Every day of it in open country. You do not need me to explain that to you.

asks.q: Do the Miami and the Potawatomi get along?
a: We are neighbours, which means we sometimes do and sometimes do not. The Potawatomi came south into country that was once ours. We have married each other's daughters for a hundred years. We have also stolen each other's horses for a hundred years. Both things are true at once.

more.q: Do you have cousins in the camps?
a: Yes. I saw one this morning by the river. He looked at me and I looked at him and neither of us said a word. Tomorrow we may be on different sides of the same field. Tonight we are just two men who know each other's mothers.

asks.q: Have you fought before?
a: At the Fallen Timbers, eighteen summers ago, when I was very young, against General Wayne's soldiers. The Americans won. The nations made the treaty at Greenville. Since then the Miami have kept the peace, as Little Turtle said we should.

more.q: Was it hard to make peace with men you had fought?
a: Hard? It was the hardest thing my people ever did. But Little Turtle was right: the Americans were too many. You can fight a war you can win or you can make a peace you can live with. He chose to live. Not everyone agreed with him, and not everyone does now.

asks.q: Do you know any animals?
a: Muskrats, they live in houses of mud in the marsh. Beavers, they cut down trees with their teeth. Raccoons, they wash their food. Skunks, you do not go near them. Bears, my grandfather saw one. Wolves, you hear them at night. Turtles, I caught one as big as a kettle.

more.q: What did you do with the turtle?
a: My mother made soup. I wanted to keep it. She said a turtle is not a dog. I said why not. She did not have a good answer.
The otter. It slides down the riverbank on its belly, over and over, just because it likes it. My uncle says that is a waste of time. I think the otter knows something my uncle does not.

asks.q: Does anyone tell you stories?
a: My grandmother, in the winter, when the snow is deep. Never in summer. Stories are for winter, she says, when the spirits are asleep and cannot hear us talking about them. If you tell a winter story in summer, a snake might come into your bed.
No! It is summer! You want a snake in my bed? Ask me again when it snows.

asks.q: Who do you work for?
a: For the officers' families, in the kitchen and the wash-house and the garden, from before light until after dark. Cooking, carrying, scrubbing, minding the children. The work does not stop because the army is leaving. If anything it doubles.
I go where the family goes. Nobody asked me if I wanted to. I have packed their things and then my own, which took less time.

more.q: What do you think will happen?
a: I think the people who have the least say will pay the most, as usual. I hope I am wrong. I have been wrong before, once or twice.

asks.q: Are you ready for tomorrow?
a: Ready is a big word. My musket is clean, my cartridge box holds twenty-five rounds, and that is all the captain lets a man carry. The rest went down the well last night with the spare powder. We are marching a hundred and fifty miles to Fort Wayne with women and children and wagons, through country full of men who are not our friends any more.

So it cannot be handed to the warriors who are camped round us. The captain promised them the goods in the store, and they are owed them, by his word. But he would not give them the means to shoot us. So the whiskey went in the river and the powder down the well. They saw it. They know what it means. That is the trouble.

I trust he is honest. He has been at this post for two years and he has never cheated a man. Whether he is right is another matter. Mr. Kinzie said stay, or go at once. The captain did neither for six days. Ask him yourself, if you can catch him alone. He looks tired.

asks.q: What happened to all the whiskey?
a: We poured it into the river last night. Barrels of it, broached and rolled to the bank and tipped. Some of the lads stood there with their tongues out like dogs at a butcher's door. A sergeant stood over us so nobody saved a cupful.

The whiskey was for the warriors in the camps, by the captain's promise. Mr. Kinzie argued with him all afternoon: give them whiskey and powder, he said, and you hand a drunk man a loaded gun. The captain gave way on that. So they get blankets and cloth and pots, and the river gets the rest.

Notice? The river was brown with it this morning, and people from the camps were down at the mouth tasting the water. They know what we did. A man said to me in his language what I took to be: you promised. He was right. We did.

asks.q: Who are the riders that came in yesterday?
a: That is Captain Wells, the captain's wife's uncle, come up from Fort Wayne with about thirty Miami to bring us out. He rode through the gate yesterday afternoon on a fine horse, and every man on the walls cheered. He knows this country and these people better than anybody alive.

He is everything. He was taken by the Miami as a boy, and grew up one of them, and married a chief's daughter, and fought against General St. Clair. Then he changed sides and scouted for General Wayne. Some say he is the bravest man in the West. Some say he does not know which side he is on. I say he came.

more.q: Will the Miami fight for us?
a: I hope so. There are thirty of them and four or five hundred warriors in the camps round the fort. You can do that arithmetic as well as I can. Go and ask Captain Wells. He tells you the truth even when you do not want it.

asks.q: That's a strange hat. What is it?
a: It is a shako, a tall felt hat, black, with a plate on the front and a plume. In the sun it cooks your head and in the wind it tries to leave. On the march tomorrow I shall have it tied on with a string, like a child's bonnet.

Blue wool, faced red, buttoned up to the collar, in August. The quartermaster has not sent new ones in two years, so mine is patched at both elbows and one sleeve is shorter than the other. Private Crozier mends them. He was a tailor before he enlisted. Ask him to show you his needle case.

Because a soldier in his coat is a soldier, and a man in his shirt is just a man. When the column goes out tomorrow morning, the people in the camps will count blue coats. We want them to count every one.

asks.q: What does a soldier do here all day?
a: Mostly not fight. We drill in the morning, cut wood, haul water, hoe the garden, mend the pickets, mend the roofs, and stand guard at night. Some of us were farmers before and we keep the fort's cattle. Some were nothing in particular, and we do the digging.

Dull until this summer. Now every shadow by the river is something. A man on the north-east blockhouse at night sees a hundred things that are not there and one that is. You learn to tell the owl from the man imitating one.

The garden. We grew good corn and potatoes and melons here. Elias Mills has been at the wagons all day, and he grumbles that he will never taste our melons again. Go and see him at the wagon. He will tell you about the oxen. Do not let him tell you about the melons. You will be there all night.

asks.q: Who is everyone so afraid of?
a: Tecumseh, if you want a name. The Shawnee who has been riding from nation to nation for years, telling every people from the lakes to the gulf to stand together against the Americans. His brother the Prophet has the visions. Tecumseh has the plan. He has gone over to the British now.

No, and I hope I never will. But I have seen what his word does. The young men in the camps round us listen to it. Even the old chiefs who are our friends cannot hold them. They say Mackinac has fallen to the British without a shot. They say Detroit is next.

The Potawatomi war leader from the Kankakee. He hates us more than Tecumseh does, if that is possible, and he does not care who knows it. He went north to fight with the British. His young men are some of the ones watching the fort. If you see a man with a red sash looking at you very steadily, step back.

asks.q: Do you have family here?
a: Not me. But half the men in the garrison do, or near enough. There are nine wives in the fort and eighteen children, give or take, and every one of them will march out with us tomorrow, in the wagons or on foot. The married men have been quiet all day.

In the wagons, with the sick and the baggage. Mrs. Burns has a new baby, so new it barely has a name, and she will be carried in her bed. The rest of the children will be packed in like apples. Go and see her if you like. She is calm, which is more than I can say for the rest of us.
I would like you to tell me so. I would believe it from a stranger more than from a sergeant.

asks.q: Has anyone tried to run?
a: Not yet. Where would he run to? Out there is a hundred and fifty miles of prairie and woods and nobody friendly between here and Fort Wayne. In here is the captain and his orders and a dry roof. A man can hate both and still choose the roof.

Most of us. Behind these walls, with the guns and the stores, we could hold for months. That is what Mr. Kinzie and the young officers wanted. The captain has his orders from General Hull, and he says an order is an order. He may be right. I will tell you on Saturday.

In front of us, nothing. Behind the door of the captain's quarters, plenty, if the cook is to be believed. Ensign Ronan is young and hot and says we should fight our way out with our heads up. Lieutenant Helm says nothing at all and looks at his wife.

asks.q: What do they feed you?
a: Salt pork, flour, beans, and whatever we grow or shoot. Beef when a steer is killed. Corn and fish from the people in the camps when they were still friendly. We baked bread in the fort's ovens every day. We will be eating hardtack and cold pork on the road.

In the spring, when the supply ship was late, we had pork and nothing else for a month. Mr. Kinzie sold the fort flour from his own store and was paid in promises from Washington. He has been paid in promises for years. Go and ask him about it. He can make a joke of anything except that.

more.q: Do you trade with the camps?
a: We used to. A twist of tobacco for a basket of corn, a knife for a string of fish. This summer the camps stopped trading. That was the first sign, the old soldiers say. When the corn stops coming in, the friendship has already gone out.

asks.q: Who beats the drum at dawn?
a: We have a drummer and a fifer and they wake the whole country at dawn whether it wants to be woken or not. Reveille, then the call to drill, then the call to dinner, then tattoo at night. A soldier's day is cut into pieces by a boy with two sticks.

They will play us out of the gate. The captain wants us to march out in order, colours flying, drums going, as a garrison should. Some say it is a brave idea and some say it is like ringing a bell to tell the wolves where the sheep are. Both are true.

A young man, but he looks a boy. Go and find John Hamilton if you want to know about the post's music. He knows every call and he will tell you which of them he hates. I think it is reveille. Everybody hates reveille.

asks.q: What do you think of the young ensign?
a: Ensign Ronan? He came to us straight from the military academy at West Point, and he is as straight as a ramrod and about as bendable. He thinks the captain is too timid. He says so, which young officers are not supposed to do.

He is brave. Whether a man is a good officer is something you find out on a bad day, and he has not had one yet. I would rather have him beside me than behind me. Go and talk to him. He will be glad of somebody to argue with who is not the captain.

The men like an officer who calls them by their names, and he does. He calls me Private and then my name, every time, like a schoolmaster. It makes you stand up straighter. Do not tell him I said that.

asks.q: How did the order to leave get here?
a: A Potawatomi man named Winnemeg carried it from General Hull at Detroit, through the woods, alone, with the letter sewn into his clothes. He came in on the ninth. Five days ago. Every day since, the camps round us have filled up a little more.

He told the captain to go at once, the next morning, before the warriors could gather, or else to stay inside the fort and hold it. Mr. Kinzie said the same. The captain waited for Captain Wells and for the goods to be handed out. Now here we are, the night before, with the camps full.

Somewhere in the fort or near it, I think. He is a brave man and a friend, and his own people are not pleased with him for carrying American letters. Go and look for him. Thank him from the garrison, if he will hear it.

asks.q: Do the men gamble?
a: When the officers are not looking, which is most of the time. Cards, dice, a game with knucklebones that a Canadian taught us. We play for tobacco and buttons and a promise of tomorrow's whiskey ration, which nobody will get now.

There is a private from Kentucky who never loses. He says he was raised by a riverboat gambler. He owes nobody anything and everybody owes him something. Tonight he forgave every debt in the barracks. Nobody said why. Nobody needed to.

Write a letter, if I can borrow a pen. Not that there is anywhere to send it. I will give it to someone and ask them to carry it, if they get somewhere and I do not. It is what you do the night before.

asks.q: Where are you from, before the army?
a: County Tyrone, by way of Philadelphia, by way of a recruiting sergeant and a pint of rum. I signed for five years and I have done four of them, and I have seen more of America from inside a blue coat than most Americans ever will.

I liked it. The lake is like the sea at home, grey and cold and full of moods. The prairie in June is a garden nobody planted. If I come through this, I might take up land here myself one day. A man could farm this country if he was let alone.

A Potawatomi lad about my age who used to bring fish to the gate. We had about twenty words in common and we used them all. He has not come this week. I hope it is because he is ashamed, and not because he is angry.

asks.q: What was decided at the council?
a: Two days ago the captain met the chiefs outside the fort. He told them he would give them the goods in the store, the cloth and blankets and provisions, and that they in turn would give his people safe escort to Fort Wayne. The chiefs agreed. Then the captain decided the whiskey and the powder would not be part of it.

Some of the old chiefs meant it, I am certain. Black Partridge meant it. Whether they can make their young men keep it is another thing. A chief among the Potawatomi leads by persuasion, not command. And persuasion has been going the other way all summer.

more.q: Why did the young officers stay away?
a: Because the captain would not order the cannon trained on the council, and they thought he was walking into a trap. He went anyway, with the gate open behind him. Whatever you think of his judgment, that took courage. Ask him about it. He will shrug.

asks.q: Are you a soldier too?
a: Not in the way they are. I am one of the twelve men of the settlement that the captain has made a militia company, with Thomas Burns as our sergeant. We have muskets from the fort's store. We drilled for three days. Before that I was a farmer, and a cooper, and a man who could shoot a deer.

more.q: Will you march with the army?
a: Beside the wagons. Our wives and children are in them. The regulars march in front and behind, and the Miami ride ahead with Captain Wells. We are the ones who stay with the families no matter what. That is the only thing we were asked to do, and the only thing we would agree to.

more.q: What will happen to your farm?
a: It is already gone, as far as I am concerned. The cattle will be killed or taken, the house burned or lived in by somebody else. I have a cow named Patience. I hope whoever takes her treats her well. She deserves it more than I do.

asks.q: When did people here start to be afraid?
a: In April, at Lee's farm on the South Branch. A party of strangers came in friendly, sat by the fire, and then turned on the men there. Two were killed: Liberty White and a Canadian named Cardin. A boy and the discharged soldier John Kelso ran all the way to the fort to give the alarm.

Every family in the settlement came inside the fort that night, and most have been inside or close by ever since. The captain sent out soldiers at first light. They found what they found. Mr. Lee has not been back to his farm. Go and talk to him if you can. He does not say much about it.

more.q: Were the men who did it from the camps here?
a: They were not from the villages close by, as far as anybody could tell. Winnebago, people said, though nobody knows for sure. But after that night, every visitor at the gate was a stranger until he proved otherwise. That is a terrible way to live beside your neighbours.

asks.q: Where do you live?
a: On the north bank of the river, across from the fort, where the Kinzies and the Ouilmettes and a few more families have their houses. We cross by canoe. There is no bridge, and the river is deep enough to drown a careless man.

Mr. Kinzie, the trader, with the big house and the poplars. The Ouilmettes, Antoine and his wife Archange, who has more relations in the camps than anyone. Antoine says he is staying behind when we leave. He says nobody will hurt a man who has never hurt anybody. I hope he is right. Go and ask him.

more.q: What will you take with you?
a: What fits in a wagon. My wife has packed the Bible, the good knife, her mother's spoons, a sack of meal and the baby's things. I am taking my axe. A man with an axe can make anything again except a house.

asks.q: What is it like for the women in the fort?
a: Crowded. We have been inside the walls since April, mostly, sleeping in the barracks or in the officers' houses, cooking for our families over somebody else's fire. Mrs. Heald and Mrs. Helm keep us organised. Without them I think we would have murdered each other by June.

I am afraid all the time and I have been since April. You get used to it, the way you get used to a toothache. It is there when you wake up and it is there when you go to sleep. Tonight it is very loud.

My children, my spoons, my good shawl and my husband's Bible. I sewed my rings into the hem of my petticoat. Mrs. Heald says that is clever. She sewed hers into her stays. Go and ask her what she is wearing tomorrow. She is going to ride, did you know? On horseback, beside her husband.

asks.q: What will you miss most?
a: My garden. Beans, squash, cabbages, onions, a row of sunflowers taller than my husband. I put in roses from my mother's cuttings that came all the way from Ohio in a bucket. They bloomed for the first time this June. Pink ones.
If the government comes back, perhaps. If not, the roses will grow wild and the deer will eat the beans and the prairie will take the rest in two summers. A garden needs a woman the way a baby does.

more.q: Is anyone else leaving a garden?
a: Everyone. Mrs. Simmons is leaving her house and her husband's cattle, and she has a baby girl at her breast and a little boy hanging on her skirt. Go and see her. She will tell you what she is packing. I think she is more frightened than she lets on, and braver.

asks.q: What are you cooking tonight?
a: Everything in the house that will not travel. The last of the eggs, a ham we were saving, the good flour made into bread that will be stale by Monday. We will eat well tonight and badly for a month. That is how you leave a place.

Cicely, who belongs to the captain and his wife, which is to say she does all their work and they own her and her baby. She makes the best biscuits in the fort and she never gets any credit. If you go to the captain's quarters, look in the kitchen. Do not tell her I sent you.
Whatever they can steal from my table before I turn round. Tonight I will let them. Tomorrow I will need them strong.

asks.q: What do you think of Mrs. Heald?
a: She is a Kentucky girl, Captain Wells's niece, and she rides a horse better than her husband does. She married him at twenty and came here on horseback through the woods with her servant Cicely. She has a temper, but she is fair, and she has never once looked down on any of us.

If she is, she hides it in front of us. Her uncle came to bring her out. She told me she cried when she saw him ride in, because she knew he would not have come so far unless he thought she was in danger. Then she dried her eyes and went to see about the bread.

more.q: Will she ride with the army?
a: She will. In front, with her husband and her uncle. She says if it comes to it, she will not be carried in a wagon like a sack of flour. Go and ask her yourself. She will tell you what she thinks of wagons.

asks.q: What is your work here?
a: I am an engagé, a hired man, for Mr. Kinzie. I paddle his canoes, carry his packs over the portage to the Des Plaines, and take his trade goods to the winter camps on the Illinois and the Rock River. Ninety pounds on my back and a song in my mouth, that is how we go.

The path from the South Branch of this river, across a little marsh, to the Des Plaines, which runs down to the Illinois and the Mississippi. In spring when the water is high you can paddle almost the whole way. In August you drag the canoe through mud up to your knees and the mosquitoes eat you alive.

more.q: Will you go with the army?
a: No. Mr. Kinzie is sending his family round by boat, and I will be in that boat. Then, who knows? The French have lived here before the Americans and we will be here after. Go and ask the master. He will tell you about the portage. He has walked it more times than I have.

asks.q: Do you know any songs?
a: Every engagé knows a hundred. You sing to keep the paddles together, twenty strokes a minute, all day long. À la claire fontaine. En roulant ma boule. The boss likes a fast song when he is late and a slow one when he is tired.

Not tonight. Tonight nobody sings. But I will tell you the words of one: by the clear fountain, I went to walk, and the water was so lovely that I bathed in it. It is a love song. Everything we sing is a love song, even when we are carrying ninety pounds of lead.

Pierre Le Clerc, who is part Potawatomi and part French and has a voice like a church bell. Go and find him. Ask him for the song about the girl from Montreal. If he is in the mood, he will sing it. Tonight he is not in the mood.

asks.q: Whose side are you on?
a: The side of the canoe. That is a joke, but not much of one. My mother is Ottawa. My father was a voyageur from Trois-Rivières. My wife is Potawatomi. My employer is Mr. Kinzie, who is British by birth and American by business. I am on the side of not getting killed and keeping my family fed.

If they take Detroit, they will have all the lakes. Then the Americans will come back, because they always come back, with more men. The fur trade will go on whoever wins. Somebody always needs a man who can paddle and speak four languages.

more.q: What do your wife's people say?
a: That the Americans take land and the British only take furs. That is the whole argument, in one sentence. I cannot tell them they are wrong.

asks.q: Why did you come all this way?
a: We came with Apekonit, whom the Americans call William Wells. He asked, and we came. He is our relative by marriage; his wife was the daughter of the great war leader Little Turtle, who died this summer. We rode from Fort Wayne in a few days, fast.

more.q: Will you fight for the Americans?
a: We came to bring the soldiers and the women out to Fort Wayne. That is what we agreed to. Whether we fight depends on what happens on the road. There are thirty of us and many hundreds of Potawatomi, and some of those Potawatomi are our friends, and some of them are our cousins. You see the problem.

He says little. He has been very quiet since we rode in. Tonight he sits with his niece and her husband. Tomorrow he will lead the column. Go and look at him. You will see a man who has made up his mind about something.

asks.q: Who was Little Turtle?
a: The greatest war leader the Miami ever had. Twenty-one years ago he beat General St. Clair's army on the Wabash, the worst defeat the Americans ever had from our people. Then he saw that we could not keep winning, and he made peace at Greenville, and he kept it until he died, this July, at Fort Wayne.

more.q: How is he related to Wells?
a: Wells married his daughter. Wells fought beside him against St. Clair, and then went over to the Americans and scouted against him for Wayne. Little Turtle forgave him. That tells you something about both of them. Ask Wells about his father-in-law. He will not refuse.

He knew him and did not join him. He said the Shawnee's path led to the destruction of all our nations. Tecumseh said Little Turtle had become an American. They were both right, in their way, which is the worst kind of quarrel.

asks.q: Why have so many people come to the fort?
a: Because the captain has promised goods to everyone, and because word came that the soldiers are leaving. There are people here from the villages on the Fox, the Kankakee, the Calumet, the Des Plaines, the Milwaukee. Some came for the blankets. Some came for other reasons.

The soldiers poured the whiskey into the river and the powder down the well. They promised and then took back. The young men have been listening to Tecumseh's messengers all summer, and to Main Poc's. Mackinac has fallen. Detroit is next. A young man who wants to be a warrior will not have a better chance than tomorrow.

more.q: What do the old men say?
a: Black Partridge, from the Illinois River, says keep the peace. He has kept it for seventeen years. Tonight he will go to the captain and give back his medal. Go and see him do it. It will be the saddest thing you see this summer, and there will be many.

asks.q: What do your people trade with the Americans?
a: Furs. Muskrat, beaver, otter, mink, raccoon, deer hides. We bring them to the trader Kinzie and he gives us cloth, kettles, knives, guns, powder, silver, blankets. In a good winter a family can trap enough to buy everything it needs for a year.

Kinzie is fairer than most. He gives credit in the autumn and takes the furs in the spring, and if a family has a bad winter he waits. He speaks our language. He has a temper. This June he killed a man, Lalime, in a fight by the fort. People still argue about that. Go and ask him what happened, if you dare.

more.q: What will happen to the trade now?
a: If the Americans go, the British traders will come back from the north. They give better presents. They do not want our land, only our furs. That is what my uncle says. I am not sure he is right, but I am not sure he is wrong.

asks.q: What is good hunting here?
a: Deer in the oak groves along the river, all year. Ducks and geese by the thousand in spring and autumn, on the marshes west of here. Fish in the lake and the rivers: sturgeon, whitefish, pike. In the winter, our men go far out on the prairie for the elk and buffalo, though there are fewer buffalo every year.

The marsh at the head of the South Branch, where the portage goes over to the Des Plaines. In October the sky goes black with ducks. You can hear them a mile off. Waubansee, from the Fox River, knows it better than I do. Ask him about the year the geese came so thick they broke the trees.
My mother's brother. That is how it is with us. Your father loves you and your uncle teaches you. He taught me to wait. Most of hunting is waiting.

asks.q: What do you think of Tecumseh?
a: He is the greatest speaker I have ever heard. Two summers ago he came to a council on the Fox River and talked for a whole afternoon, and nobody moved. He said the land belongs to all the nations together, and no one nation can sell it. He said the Americans will not stop until they reach the western sea.

I look at the treaties. Every few years, another treaty, another piece of land, another promise. My father's village was on land the Americans now call theirs. Tecumseh did not invent that. He only said it out loud.

Black Bird, of the Milwaukee people, is a war leader now. He has many young men around him in the camps. Go and look for him, and look carefully. He is not your friend. He would want you to know that.

asks.q: What does a chief's medal mean?
a: It is a silver medal with the face of the American President on it, given at a treaty to a man the Americans want to treat as a chief. To the Americans it means: this man is our friend and speaks for his people. To us it means: this man made a promise, and wears it on his chest.

more.q: Can a man give it back?
a: He can, if he cannot keep the promise any more. Black Partridge is going to give his back tonight. He will tell the captain that his young men will not be held. He is giving back the medal so that he does not have to lie with it on his chest. It is a terrible honesty.

He will not fight against the Americans, I think. He will do what he can for them, if he can. That is a different thing from what the medal promised, and it is all an honest man has left. Go and see him at the captain's quarters tonight.

asks.q: How is your lodge made?
a: In summer we live in long houses of bark and mats over bent saplings, by the river, near the cornfields. In winter we break into small family camps in the woods and live in round lodges covered with cattail mats, warm and dark, with the fire in the middle and the smoke going out at the top.

The women. The women own the lodges, the mats, the kettles and the fields. The men hunt and fish and go to war and talk in councils. A man who forgets who owns the lodge does not sleep in it for long.

Go down to the camps by the river, but go with someone known. Archange Ouilmette, whose husband is the Frenchman across the river, has relations in every lodge here. Go with her, and they will give you food. Go alone, tonight, and nobody can tell you what will happen.

asks.q: Will you fight tomorrow?
a: You ask me that straight to my face? You are bold. I will tell you this: I have been told by my elders to keep the peace and by Tecumseh's messengers to take back our country, and I have been told by the soldiers that they would give us whiskey and powder, and then they threw them in the river.
I will do what the men of my village decide in council tonight. A man alone is nothing. A man with his village is a nation. Ask me again tomorrow evening, if we both see it.
Some of them I like. One of them used to trade me fish hooks for corn. I hope he goes back to wherever he came from and stays there. That is not hate. That is wishing him well.

asks.q: What is the best time of year?
a: Sugar time, in the spring, when the snow is still on the ground and the maple sap is running. The whole village goes to the sugar bush and the women boil sap day and night in big kettles over fires, and the children run around with sticky hands and nobody sleeps much.

Better than anything the traders sell. We pour it into moulds of birch bark and make cakes, and we keep it all year to season everything, even the fish. A Frenchman told me his people eat it on bread. That seemed strange to me. Now I do it too.

The end of winter, before sugar, when the dried corn is running out and the hunting is poor and the children are thin. That is when you learn who your relatives are. Everybody shares or everybody starves.

asks.q: How did you get your name?
a: Every child is named by an elder who has dreamed the name, a few days after the birth. The name comes from the spirits, so it is not to be joked about. A man may get another name later, for something he does, and use that instead.

more.q: Do the Americans use your name?
a: They write it down in their own letters and it comes out wrong every time. Topenebe, the old chief of the St. Joseph villages, has been written five different ways in the treaties, and none of them is how his mother said it. Ask him what his name means. He will tell you, if he likes you.

more.q: Do you have an American name?
